facts.statement: Meridiocichla was an extinct genus of large thrushes that lived in Southern Europe during the Late Quaternary period.
facts.quote: Meridiocichla is an extinct genus of large thrush that inhabited Southern Europe during the Late Quaternary period.

facts.statement: The only species, M. salotti, was the largest known thrush from Europe, roughly the size of a scaly thrush.
facts.quote: The sole species, M. salotti, is the largest known thrush from Europe, being about the size of a scaly thrush (Zoothera dauma).

facts.statement: The only known fossils of Meridiocichla were found on the Mediterranean islands of Corsica and Crete.
facts.quote: The only known fossils of Meridiocichla come from the islands of Corsica and Crete in the Mediterranean Sea.

facts.statement: Fossils from Corsica include a premaxillary bone from Funtanedu Cave and humeri from Coscia Cave, while Crete yielded finds from Liko Cave.
facts.quote: The fossils from Corsica constituted a premaxillary bone from Funtanedu Cave (dated to the Late Pleistocene or Holocene) and two humeri from Coscia Cave (Late Pleistocene), while the findings in Crete were from Liko Cave (Late Pleistocene).

facts.statement: The species was assigned to its own genus primarily because it had a large body size combined with a short, robust beak.
facts.quote: The fossils were formally described and assigned to their own genus, Meridiocichla, mostly due to differences in beak morphology: the species had a large body size but with a short yet robust beak.

facts.statement: The genus name Meridiocichla combines the Latin word for 'southern' and the Greek word for 'thrush'.
facts.quote: The generic name Meridiocichla is a combination of the Latin word meridionalis, meaning "southern" (in reference to its Mediterranean distribution), and the Greek word kikhle, meaning "thrush".

facts.statement: The specific name commemorates paleontologist and archaeologist Michelle Salotti.
facts.quote: The specific epithet commemorates paleontologist and archeologist Michelle Salotti.

facts.statement: Meridiocichla was an omnivore, similar to other thrushes.
facts.quote: Like other thrushes, it was an omnivore.

facts.statement: Despite its large size and island habitat, fossils show no evidence that Meridiocichla was flightless.
facts.quote: Despite the bird's large size and insular habitat, there were no signs of flightlessness in the fossils found.

facts.statement: It is unlikely the species was restricted only to Corsica and Crete, given unconfirmed remains from continental France, Italy, and Mallorca.
facts.quote: It is unlikely that the species was limited to just Corsica and Crete, due to both the distance between the islands and due to there being several unconfirmed remains from continental France and Italy, as well as Mallorca.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the Mediterranean islands may have served as wintering grounds rather than permanent habitats.
facts.quote: Instead, the Mediterranean islands may have simply served as part of the species' wintering grounds.

facts.statement: The exact phylogenetic relationships of Meridiocichla to other thrush species remain unclear.
facts.quote: Its phylogenetic relations to other thrush species are unclear.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Meridiocichla belongs to the thrush family or is related to Old World flycatchers and whistling thrushes based on humerus comparisons.
facts.quote: direct comparisons of humeri proved an exact match to large thrushes of the genera Turdus and Zoothera, but also to the Old World flycatcher genus Myophonus, the whistling thrushes.

facts.statement: Meridiocichla was already rare during the Late Pleistocene and went extinct during the Late Pleistocene extinctions.
facts.quote: Meridiocichla appeared to have been already rare during the Late Pleistocene, and its disappearance coincided with the Late Pleistocene extinctions.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest its large size may have contributed to extinction by lowering population densities and making it vulnerable to sudden threats on islands.
facts.quote: Like the Pleistocene megafauna, its large size may have played a role in its extinction, due to larger species having lower population densities and lower local population sizes, especially on islands, where insular species can be particularly vulnerable to sudden threats.

facts.statement: Meridiocichla is classified within the family Turdidae.
Meridiocichla lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Late Pleistocene to Holocene (0.129 to 0 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Corsican fossils were described as very large with a bill larger than that of the mistle thrush.
rejected.quote: The Corsican fossils were labeled as "very large" and as having a bill larger than that of the mistle thrush (Turdus viscivorus).
